[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Satan who whispered to the pair was Iblis alone.
[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Satan sought to expose what had been concealed from them, namely their nakedness.
[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | Iblis told them that he had been created before them, knew more than they did, and that obeying him would guide them.
[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Iblis claimed God forbade the tree only to keep them from becoming angels or from attaining immortality; if not angels, they would be immortal.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A phrase used as a name may be preserved exactly as it was in ordinary speech; examples include taʾabbaṭa sharran and barq naḥruhu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Phrases such as lā khayran minhu laka and lā ḍāriban rajulan laka show that tanwīn remains in these quoted constructions.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names formed from two separate words such as ʿāqilatun labībatun and ʿāqilun labībun keep each word's ordinary inflection and tanwīn.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | For a single feminine name ʿĀqila, quoting the indefinite form may be allowed, but the preferred form drops tanwīn; the two-word phrase is best treated as a quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl treats min Zayd and ʿan Zayd as changed compound names, not ordinary case-governed phrases, because these prepositions depend on a complement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A compound like wazn sabʿa or khamsata ʿashar is treated as a compound proper name, not as a preserved utterance.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl treats fī Zayd as a heavy compound name; its final yā can be mobile in the accusative, unlike the separate min and ʿan compounds.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Inna-ma, anna-ma, kaʾanna-ma, ḥaythu-ma, and imma remain quoted forms because mā is not fused into a single word as in ḥaḍramawt.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | The mā in ḥaythu-ma does not remove the dialectal forms of ḥayth; it instead blocks an from the subjunctive and makes ḥayth conditional.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unnamed poet's in jazʿan wa-in ijmāl ṣabr is cited to show that the form represents imma.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh says exception illā is like duflā; in 7:20 the form is the exception particle.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A line attributed to a poet from Banū Ṭahiyya leaves dharā ḥubban intact, illustrating a phrase used as a name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Illā and immā in conditional constructions are treated as quotations.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Amma in ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliq is not quoted and is like shurwā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Interrogative ammā and allā are quoted forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Allā innahu ẓarīf and ammā innahu ẓarīf behave like qafā and raḥā; laʿalla and forms with added kāf or tā remain quoted.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hādhā and hāʾulāʾi keep their ordinary form as names because retaining the hāʾ of attention preserves the quoted expression.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh reports hallum as quoted in both dialects; the Tāmīmī hallumman form supports that analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Lawma, lawla, and the heard phrase lā min ayna are preserved as quotations rather than converted into ordinary names.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as bū Zayd and wa-Zaydan follow their phrase form because these particles occur only as dependents.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Zayd al-ṭawīl as a name remains a quotation; if al-ṭawīl is made a true adjective, it inflects, and vocative form changes according to whether the whole phrase is called.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A relative phrase such as al-ladhī raʾaytu stays unchanged because the relative clause completes one name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Changing a quoted phrase when it becomes a name would produce forms people do not use, such as turning a verse into an altered name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The phrase al-rajul munṭaliqun can be called because it consists of two complete words.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The relative name cannot take yā ayyuha because it is a single proper name, like al-Naḍr.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Long coordinated names can revert to ordinary case marking in the vocative; the first item is tanwīnated when it is not the endpoint of the full name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the first part is a feminine proper name such as Ṭalḥa or Ḥamza, its vocative has no tanwīn, while Zaydan and ʿAmran take it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r34] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kā-Zayd and bi-Zayd are quotations because separating kāf or bāʾ would change their form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r35] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A name ʿAm can preserve its interrogative form; if the speaker instead makes it an independent noun, the phrase becomes ʿan māʾ and is lengthened.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r36] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When ʿan māʾ is turned into an independent name, it is lengthened and treated as a compound, like the naming construction ʿan Zayd.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unnamed poet's line beginning kadhabtum wa-bayti Allāh is another example of a phrase preserved as a name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A poet's phrase aḥaqq al-khayli bi-l-rakḍ al-muʿār is cited as another unchanged quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Quoted names are not dualized or pluralized internally; an outer kull or kilā may be added while the quoted phrase stays unchanged.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Quoted names are not annexed or diminished; a shortened form may be made by deleting part and treating the remainder like an annexed form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Multiword names such as khayrun minka, maʾkhūdhun bika, and ḍāriban rajulan retain their ordinary phrase form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحكايةالتيلاتغيرفيهاالأسماءعنحالهافيالكلام)#555/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says a woman named khayrun minka or ḍāriban rajulan keeps tanwīn because the phrase is not complete at khayr or ḍārib.
[MAJAZ:v1p211/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Qāsamahumā means he swore an oath to them both; elsewhere the root can refer to dividing shares.
[AKHFASH:v1p322/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Waswasa lahumā means waswasa ilayhimā; Arabic verbs can take varied prepositions, as ghariḍtu can mean I longed for him, literally from these toward him.
[AKHFASH:v1p322/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The exception means he forbade them only out of aversion to their becoming angels, like the idiom iyyāka an tafʿala for fear or dislike of doing something.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p166#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Li-yubdiya means to reveal or make apparent.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p166#2/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Wūriya means was hidden; tawārī and muwārāh derive from the same root.
[TUSTARI:7:20/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Whispering unfolds through natural disposition, then the soul, then inward concern and planning.
[TUSTARI:7:20/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | The enemy's whisper has three stages: invitation, confidence once someone accepts, and finally waiting and hoping for an opening, as with the truthful.
[TAB-FULL:v10p106#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The whisper was Satan’s lie to the

 pair that their Lord forbade the tree only to keep them from becoming angels or immortals, accompanied by an oath.
[TAB-FULL:v10p106#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The construction وسوس لهما means that Satan whispered from himself to them; Tabari compares it to غرضت له, glossed as اشتقت إليه, while clarifying the underlying direction with غرضت من هؤلاء إليه, and cites Ruʾba’s line using وسوس.
[TAB-FULL:v10p106#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb ibn Munabbih says the covering God placed over Adam and his wife was a light through which their nakedness could not be seen. | mentions 20:121
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Satan tells Adam and Eve that God prohibited eating the tree so they would not become angels or immortals.
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The wording omits لا, understood from context, as in 4:176, where the sense is that God explains so people will not go astray. | mentions 4:176
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل العربية من أهل البصرة | reports | A Basran grammarian takes the exception as expressing aversion: God forbade the tree because He disliked their becoming angels, by analogy with a warning given out of fear of an outcome.
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس ويحيى بن أبي كثير | reports | Ibn Abbas and Yaḥyā b. Abī Kathīr are reported to read malikayn with kasra, meaning two kings; they connect this interpretation to the imperishable dominion of 20:120. | mentions 20:120
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī insists on the widely transmitted regional reading with fatḥa, meaning two angels, and says no other reading is permissible.
[TAB-FULL:v10p108/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The immortals are those who remain in Paradise forever and do not die.
[ZAJJAJ:v2p326/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | The word may be read as ملكين, angels; the phrase ملك لا يبلى in the tree-of-immortality passage supports it, and al-Zajjaj thinks this reading may have been recited. | mentions 20:120
[ZAJJAJ:v2p326/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The wording indicates that the claim was Satan's whisper; the preferred construction is direct address, supported by his oath that he was a sincere adviser. | mentions 7:21
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima says Satan is so named because he became satanic.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says Satan exposed their private parts by tearing their clothing; he knew of their nakedness from angelic books, while Adam did not, and their clothing was their nails.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Satan spoke to Adam and his wife from inside a serpent after they did not believe his claim.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains “two angels” as their becoming angels like God.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says Satan described the angels' superiority in form, wings, and honor to entice Adam and his wife toward becoming angels.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid read malakayn with fatḥa on the lām, meaning two angels; Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, and al-Aʿraj report similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن منبه | reports | Ibn Munabbih says one branch of a Garden tree was circled by angels, and Satan's promise that they would become angels referred to those angels.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1450/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī glosses becoming among the immortal as never dying; Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī and Wahb ibn Munabbih report the same.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash explains lahumā as referring to Adam and his wife.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | The passive verb may appear in non-Quranic usage as ūri, like uqqitat.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Malakayni is the predicate of takūnā; an means ‘for fear of’ or ‘to avoid,’ while Kufans explain it as ‘lest.’
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · يحيى بن أبي كثير والضحاك | reports | Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and al-Dahhak read malikeen with kasra on the lām, meaning two kings rather than two angels.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو عبيد | rejects | Abu Ubayd calls the variant supported by the line ‘a kingdom that does not perish’; Abu Jaʿfar calls it anomalous and rejects this argument.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو جعفر | rejects | Abu Jaʿfar says Adam could not imagine reaching a station above Paradise’s angels; the line instead means permanence in the kingdom of Paradise.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says angels are favored with forms, wings, and honor; another view says their superiority lies in obedience and avoiding sin. | mentions 11:31, 4:172
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The preceding expression conveys the speech of someone grieving over what befell him and distressed by what touched him.
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Divine creative command is illustrated by God's command to be, the transformation into apes, and Moses' striking the sea, which then parts. | mentions 36:82, 7:166, 26:63
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Bāqillānī chose al-Buhturī's poetry because contemporaries ranked it highly and some exaggeratedly called it miraculous; he sets its real rank below God's incomparable speech.
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | His book briefly clarifies Quranic inimitability; detailed attacks on alleged errors were already handled by literary scholars and theologians, and ignorance of Arabic meaning and usage fuels many attacks.
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet compares the superiority of God's speech over all speech to God's superiority over His creation.
[BAQILLANI:v1p245/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Judging Quranic eloquence requires trained literary discernment, including the ability to rank poets and recognize Musaylima's absurd imitation.
[SULAMI:v1p223/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو سليمان الداراني | reports | Abu Sulayman al-Darani says Satan intended evil, yet his whisper became the cause of Adam's elevation; the lapse disciplined Adam and returned him to God's favor, as he confessed his wrong and sought God (7:23). | mentions 7:23
[SULAMI:v1p223/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل | reports | Sahl describes whispering as a progression from natural disposition to the self, then thought and planning.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | وسوس means the devil spoke secretly to Adam and Eve.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The devil sought to reveal the nakedness that had been covered and concealed from them.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · وهب | reports | Wahb says a light covered Adam and Eve so they could not see their nakedness.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The devil’s claim portrayed the prohibition as keeping them from becoming angels, who do good and evil.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس والضحاك ويحيى بن أبي معين | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Yahya ibn Abi Muʿayn read ملكين with kasra on the lām, meaning two kings, linked to the promised imperishable kingdom.
[THALABI:v4p223#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The alternative promise of being among the immortal means becoming those who remain and do not die.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Waswasa is a hidden-voiced summons; waswasa lahu means to make someone imagine counsel, while waswasa ilayhi means to cast a meaning into him. Ru'ba's verse uses the root for whispering.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن | reports | To explain how Satan whispered from outside the garden, al-Hasan says God gave him a power by which his whisper reached them from earth to the garden in heaven.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A second account says Satan was in heaven, while Adam and Eve went out to meet him there.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third account says Satan spoke from the garden gate while Adam and Eve remained inside.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Satan's whisper appealed to elevated status as angels and the delight of eternal life.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Their knowledge of God was complete, but their knowledge of God's rulings was not; this explains how they entertained the temptation.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One reading is that Satan falsely suggested God's law allowed their forms to change into angelic forms and that they could be made immortal.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p210/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Alternatively, Satan suggested they would attain the angels' elevated rank, while they knew a change of bodily form was not permissible.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p325/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God placed the means of trial with Adam in the Garden: his spouse and the tree of ordeal; the tree’s presence reflects the hidden mystery of divine allotment.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p325/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Although Adam and his spouse committed the lapse, God’s attribution of it to Satan is a sign of special divine care for them.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · آدم وإبليس | reports | A reported exchange has Adam blame Satan for tempting him; Satan replies that if he was Adam’s devil, Adam should ask who was his own devil.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The wording that Satan would expose their nakedness signals special care: no

 one besides Adam and his spouse saw it.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | They longed to become angels because they imagined freedom from desire and hope, not because the angelic rank exceeded Adam’s.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Their desire for immortality brought abasement, ordeal, and fear; greed is the root of every trial, and if greed in Paradise led to such trials, greed in the transient world is even less safe.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | prefers | An alternative says they sought lasting life to remain with God rather than for personal gain; Qushayri prefers it because it preserves the dignity of prophethood.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p327/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | A saying describes the span of union as brief and separation as long: Adam and his spouse entered the Garden in the morning and left at midday.
